questions.q: Who first observed and named cells, while looking at a thin slice of cork under a microscope?
questions.why: Robert Hooke saw tiny box-like compartments in cork in 1665 and called them cells. Brown later described the nucleus.

questions.q: Which organelle is the site of aerobic respiration and is called the powerhouse of the cell?
questions.why: Mitochondria carry out the later stages of aerobic respiration and release most of the cell's energy as ATP.

questions.q: Which structure is found in a plant cell but not in an animal cell?
questions.why: Only plant cells have a rigid cell wall made of cellulose outside the cell membrane; the other three are present in both.

questions.q: Which organelle is called the 'suicide bag' of the cell because its enzymes can digest the cell itself?
questions.why: Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes; if they burst, the enzymes break down the cell's own contents.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes a prokaryotic cell, such as a bacterium?
o: It has a nucleus bounded by a nuclear membrane
It is always part of a multicellular body
questions.why: In prokaryotes the DNA lies free in the cytoplasm as a nucleoid; there is no nuclear membrane and no membrane-bound organelles.

long.q: Give four differences between a typical plant cell and a typical animal cell.
scheme: B1: plant cell has a cellulose cell wall outside the cell membrane; an animal cell has only a cell membrane
B1: plant cell has plastids (chloroplasts in green parts); plastids are absent in an animal cell
B1: plant cell has a large central vacuole; an animal cell has small, temporary vacuoles or none
B1: centrosome (centrioles) is usually absent in plant cells of higher plants but present in animal cells

long.q: Name the cell organelle that: (a) is the site of protein synthesis; (b) packages and secretes substances such as enzymes; (c) contains DNA and controls all the activities of the cell; (d) forms a network of channels for transporting materials within the cytoplasm.
scheme: B1: (a) ribosome
B1: (b) Golgi apparatus (Golgi body)
B1: (c) nucleus
B1: (d) endoplasmic reticulum
long.ans: ribosome; Golgi apparatus; nucleus; endoplasmic reticulum

long.q: Explain why the cell is called the structural and functional unit of life.
scheme: B1: structural: the bodies of all living organisms are built up of cells
B1: functional: all life activities such as nutrition, respiration and excretion are carried out inside cells

long.q: State the three main points of the cell theory.
scheme: B1: all living organisms are made up of one or more cells
B1: the cell is the basic unit of structure and function of living organisms
B1: new cells arise only from pre-existing cells (by cell division)

long.q: Distinguish between the cell wall and the cell membrane with respect to (a) whether it is living, (b) chemical composition, (c) permeability.
scheme: B1: (a) the cell wall is non-living; the cell membrane is living
B1: (b) the cell wall is made mainly of cellulose; the cell membrane is made of lipids and proteins
B1: (c) the cell wall is freely (fully) permeable; the cell membrane is selectively (semi-) permeable

questions.q: Which plant tissue is responsible for increase in length at the tips of roots and shoots?
questions.why: Apical meristems at root and shoot tips keep dividing, so the plant grows in length; lateral meristem increases girth.

questions.q: Which plant tissue conducts water and minerals from the roots to the leaves?
questions.why: Xylem vessels and tracheids carry water and dissolved minerals upward; phloem carries food.

questions.q: Which tissue joins a muscle to a bone?
questions.why: A tendon is tough, inelastic connective tissue joining muscle to bone; a ligament joins bone to bone.

questions.q: Which muscle is striated, involuntary and works throughout life without tiring?
questions.why: Cardiac muscle of the heart is striated and branched, contracts rhythmically on its own and does not fatigue.

questions.q: What is the structural and functional unit of nervous tissue?
questions.why: A neuron (nerve cell) receives and conducts impulses. A nephron is the unit of the kidney.

long.q: Give three differences between meristematic tissue and permanent tissue.
scheme: B1: meristematic cells divide repeatedly; permanent tissue cells have lost the power to divide
B1: meristematic cells have dense cytoplasm, a large nucleus and no (or tiny) vacuoles; permanent cells usually have large vacuoles
B1: meristematic cells are packed closely with no intercellular spaces; permanent tissues often have intercellular spaces

long.q: Name the animal tissue that: (a) forms the protective outer layer of the skin; (b) stores fat below the skin; (c) is found in the wall of the intestine and causes peristalsis; (d) gives shape but flexibility to the external ear (pinna).
scheme: B1: (a) stratified squamous epithelium
B1: (b) adipose tissue
B1: (c) smooth (unstriated, involuntary) muscle
B1: (d) cartilage
long.ans: stratified squamous epithelium; adipose tissue; smooth muscle; cartilage

long.q: Give two reasons why blood is classed as a connective tissue.
scheme: B1: it consists of cells (red cells, white cells, platelets) lying in a fluid matrix, the plasma
B1: it connects or links all parts of the body by transporting materials between them

long.q: Describe in words the structure of a neuron and state the function of each part.
scheme: B1: cell body (cyton) containing the nucleus and cytoplasm; it controls the cell
B1: dendrites are short, branched extensions that receive impulses and carry them towards the cell body
B1: the axon is a long fibre, often covered by a myelin sheath, that carries impulses away from the cell body
B1: the axon ends in branched nerve endings that pass the impulse to the next neuron or to a muscle or gland

long.q: Name the four kinds of elements that make up phloem, and state the function of phloem.
scheme: B1: sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres (all four)
B1: phloem conducts food (sugars) made in the leaves
B1: to growing and storage parts of the plant, in both directions (translocation)

questions.q: Which whorl of a flower is its male reproductive part?
questions.why: The androecium is the whorl of stamens, which produce pollen grains containing the male gametes.

questions.q: What is the stalk of an individual flower called?
questions.why: The pedicel is the flower stalk; a petiole is a leaf stalk and the thalamus is the swollen tip that bears the floral parts.

questions.q: Which part of the pistil receives pollen grains?
questions.why: The stigma at the tip of the pistil is often sticky or feathery so that pollen grains stick to it.

questions.q: A flower that has both stamens and carpels is called:
questions.why: Bisexual (hermaphrodite) flowers have both male and female parts, as in the hibiscus.

questions.q: What is the swollen tip of the flower stalk on which all the floral whorls are borne?
questions.why: The thalamus (receptacle) carries the calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium.

long.q: Name the four whorls of a typical flower from the outside inwards and give one function of each.
scheme: B1: calyx (sepals): protects the flower in the bud stage
B1: corolla (petals): attracts insects for pollination
B1: androecium (stamens): produces pollen grains
B1: gynoecium (carpels or pistil): produces ovules and develops into the fruit after fertilisation

long.q: Describe in words the structure of a stamen.
scheme: B1: a thin stalk called the filament
B1: an anther at its tip, usually two-lobed, each lobe with pollen sacs in which pollen grains form

long.q: Explain the meaning of: (a) complete flower; (b) inflorescence; (c) unisexual flower.
scheme: B1: (a) a flower that has all four whorls: calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium
B1: (b) a group or cluster of flowers arranged on a common stalk
B1: (c) a flower that has either stamens or carpels, but not both

long.q: Give reasons: (a) petals of insect-pollinated flowers are usually large and brightly coloured; (b) sepals are usually green.
scheme: B1: (a) to attract insects, which carry pollen from flower to flower
B1: (b) they contain chlorophyll, so they can make food by photosynthesis while protecting the bud

long.q: Describe in words the structure of a carpel and state what its parts become after fertilisation.
scheme: B1: stigma: the tip, which receives pollen grains
B1: style: the stalk joining the stigma to the ovary, through which the pollen tube grows
B1: ovary: the swollen base containing one or more ovules
B1: after fertilisation the ovary becomes the fruit and the ovules become the seeds

questions.q: Transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma of the same flower is called:
questions.why: Self-pollination (autogamy) happens within one flower, or between flowers of the same plant.

questions.q: Which feature is typical of a wind-pollinated flower?
o: Light, dry pollen in large amounts and feathery stigmas
questions.why: Wind carries pollen at random, so these flowers produce huge amounts of light pollen and have feathery stigmas to catch it.

questions.q: In double fertilisation, the second male gamete fuses with:
questions.why: One male gamete fuses with the egg to form the zygote; the other fuses with the polar nuclei to form the triploid endosperm nucleus.

questions.q: After fertilisation, the integuments of the ovule develop into the:
questions.why: The integuments harden to form the seed coat (testa and tegmen); the ovary wall forms the fruit wall.

questions.q: Which of these favours cross-pollination?
o: Anthers and stigma ripening at the same time and height
Anthers and stigma maturing at different times
questions.why: When anthers and stigma ripen at different times (dichogamy), a flower's own pollen cannot fertilise it, so pollen must come from another flower.

long.q: State two advantages and one disadvantage of cross-pollination.
scheme: B1: offspring show new combinations of characters (variation)
B1: offspring are healthier and more vigorous, and better able to adapt to changes
B1: disadvantage: it depends on outside agents such as wind or insects, so it is uncertain and much pollen is wasted

long.q: Give three differences between insect-pollinated and wind-pollinated flowers.
scheme: B1: insect-pollinated flowers have large, bright petals; wind-pollinated flowers have small, dull petals or none
B1: insect-pollinated flowers have scent and nectar; wind-pollinated flowers have neither
B1: insect-pollinated flowers have fewer, sticky or spiny pollen grains; wind-pollinated flowers have large amounts of light, dry, smooth pollen

long.q: Describe in words the events from the landing of a pollen grain on a stigma to fertilisation.
scheme: B1: the pollen grain sticks to the stigma and, stimulated by its sugary secretion, germinates
B1: a pollen tube grows out and down through the style towards the ovary
B1: the generative nucleus divides to form two male gametes, which move down the tube
B1: the tube enters the ovule through the micropyle and releases the male gametes into the embryo sac
B1: one male gamete fuses with the egg to form the zygote; the other fuses with the polar nuclei to form the endosperm nucleus (double fertilisation)

long.q: State what each of the following becomes after fertilisation: (a) zygote; (b) ovary wall; (c) primary endosperm nucleus; (d) micropyle.
scheme: B1: (a) embryo
B1: (b) fruit wall (pericarp)
B1: (c) endosperm (food store of the seed)
B1: (d) remains as a small pore in the seed coat through which water enters
long.ans: embryo; pericarp; endosperm; pore in the seed coat

long.q: Give reasons: (a) maize and grasses produce very large quantities of pollen; (b) a unisexual flower cannot be self-pollinated.
scheme: B1: (a) they are wind-pollinated and wind carries pollen at random, so most of it is wasted
B1: (b) it has only stamens or only carpels, so pollen must come from another flower

questions.q: In a bean seed, the scar left where the seed was attached to the stalk is the:
questions.why: The hilum is the scar of the seed stalk; the micropyle is the tiny pore beside it.

questions.q: Which of these is a monocotyledonous seed (grain)?
questions.why: A maize grain has a single cotyledon (the scutellum); bean, pea and gram have two cotyledons.

questions.q: In which type of germination are the cotyledons pushed above the soil?
questions.why: In epigeal germination the hypocotyl lengthens and carries the cotyledons above the ground, as in bean.

questions.q: Which condition is NOT needed for the germination of most seeds?
questions.why: Most seeds germinate in the dark in soil; they need water, oxygen and warmth.

questions.q: In a maize grain, the single cotyledon is called the:
questions.why: The shield-shaped scutellum absorbs food from the endosperm for the growing embryo.

long.q: Give three differences between a bean seed and a maize grain.
scheme: B1: bean is dicotyledonous with two cotyledons; maize is monocotyledonous with one cotyledon (scutellum)
B1: bean stores food in its cotyledons (non-endospermic); maize stores food in the endosperm (endospermic)
B1: in bean the seed coat is a separate testa; in maize the seed coat is fused with the fruit wall

long.q: Describe in words an experiment to show that oxygen is necessary for germination.
scheme: B1: take two flasks, each with soaked seeds on moist cotton wool
B1: in one flask place alkaline pyrogallol solution, which absorbs oxygen, and seal it; the other flask has water instead (control)
B1: keep both flasks in the same warm place for a few days
B1: seeds in the pyrogallol flask do not germinate while the control seeds do, so oxygen is needed

long.q: Give reasons: (a) seeds are soaked in water before sowing; (b) in hypogeal germination the cotyledons stay below the soil.
scheme: B1: (a) water softens the seed coat and activates the enzymes that digest stored food
B1: (b) the epicotyl lengthens, not the hypocotyl, so only the plumule is pushed up

long.q: Name the part of the seed that: (a) gives rise to the shoot; (b) gives rise to the root; (c) lets water into the seed; (d) protects the plumule of maize as it grows up through the soil.
scheme: B1: (a) plumule
B1: (b) radicle
B1: (c) micropyle
B1: (d) coleoptile

long.q: Distinguish between epigeal and hypogeal germination, giving one example of each.
scheme: B1: epigeal: the hypocotyl lengthens and pushes the cotyledons above the soil
B1: example: bean, castor or sunflower
B1: hypogeal: the epicotyl lengthens and the cotyledons remain below the soil
B1: example: pea, gram or maize

questions.q: The products of aerobic respiration are:
questions.why: Glucose is completely oxidised to carbon dioxide and water, releasing a large amount of energy.

questions.q: Anaerobic respiration in yeast produces:
questions.why: Yeast ferments sugar to ethanol (alcohol) and carbon dioxide, which is why it is used in brewing and baking.

questions.q: Where does glycolysis, the first stage of respiration, take place?
questions.why: Glycolysis splits glucose into pyruvic acid in the cytoplasm; later aerobic stages occur in the mitochondria.

questions.q: The energy released in respiration is stored in the cell as:
questions.why: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the energy currency of the cell.

questions.q: Germinating seeds in a thermos flask with a thermometer show a rise in temperature because:
o: They absorb heat from the flask
questions.why: Some of the energy released by respiration escapes as heat; the flask stops it being lost.

long.q: Give four differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration in plants.
scheme: B1: aerobic uses oxygen; anaerobic takes place without oxygen
B1: aerobic breaks glucose down completely to carbon dioxide and water; anaerobic breaks it down incompletely to ethanol and carbon dioxide
B1: aerobic releases much energy (38 ATP per glucose); anaerobic releases little (2 ATP)
B1: aerobic occurs in cytoplasm and mitochondria; anaerobic occurs in the cytoplasm only

long.q: Write the balanced chemical equation for aerobic respiration.
scheme: B1: C₆H₁₂O₆ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O + energy (correct reactants and products)
B1: balanced: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy

long.q: Describe in words an experiment to show that germinating seeds give out carbon dioxide.
scheme: B1: place germinating seeds in a flask closed with a cork carrying a bent delivery tube
B1: the other end of the tube dips into lime water in a test tube
B1: set up a control flask with boiled (dead) seeds
B1: the lime water turns milky only with the germinating seeds, showing that carbon dioxide is released

long.q: Give reasons: (a) plants do not need special organs for breathing; (b) respiration is called a catabolic process.
scheme: B1: (a) each part exchanges gases directly by diffusion through stomata, lenticels and root hairs, and plants need relatively little oxygen
B1: (b) complex food (glucose) is broken down into simpler substances, releasing energy

long.q: Give four differences between respiration and photosynthesis.
scheme: B1: respiration releases energy (catabolic); photosynthesis stores energy in food (anabolic)
B1: respiration uses oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide; photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and gives out oxygen
B1: respiration occurs in all living cells, day and night; photosynthesis occurs only in green cells in light
B1: respiration decreases dry weight; photosynthesis increases it

questions.q: Who proposed the five kingdom classification?
questions.why: Whittaker (1969) grouped organisms into Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.

questions.q: Which kingdom contains unicellular prokaryotes such as bacteria?
questions.why: Monerans have no membrane-bound nucleus; all other kingdoms are eukaryotic.

questions.q: Which is the correct way to write the scientific name of human beings?
questions.why: The genus name starts with a capital letter and the species name with a small letter, printed in italics.

questions.q: Amoeba and Paramecium belong to the kingdom:
questions.why: They are unicellular eukaryotes, which are placed in Protista.

questions.q: The cell wall of fungi is made of:
questions.why: Fungal walls contain chitin; plant walls are mainly cellulose.

long.q: Arrange the levels of classification in order, from kingdom to species.
scheme: B1: kingdom → phylum (division) → class
B1: → order → family → genus → species, all in correct order

long.q: State three rules of binomial nomenclature.
scheme: B1: each organism has two names: the genus name followed by the species name
B1: the genus name begins with a capital letter and the species name with a small letter
B1: the name is printed in italics, or each word is underlined separately when handwritten

long.q: Name the kingdom to which each belongs and give one feature of that kingdom: (a) mushroom; (b) Euglena; (c) a bacterium; (d) a fern.
scheme: B1: (a) Fungi: heterotrophic (saprophytic) with a chitin cell wall
B1: (b) Protista: unicellular eukaryote
B1: (c) Monera: prokaryotic, with no membrane-bound nucleus
B1: (d) Plantae: multicellular, autotrophic, with cellulose cell walls

long.q: Give two advantages of classifying living organisms.
scheme: B1: it makes the study of a huge variety of organisms easier and more systematic
B1: it shows relationships between groups and helps in identifying new organisms

long.q: Name the plant group described: (a) the plant body is not divided into root, stem and leaves; (b) the 'amphibians of the plant kingdom'; (c) seeds are naked, not enclosed in a fruit; (d) seeds are enclosed in a fruit.
scheme: B1: (a) Thallophyta (algae)
B1: (b) Bryophyta (mosses)
B1: (c) Gymnosperms
B1: (d) Angiosperms

topics.name: Economic importance of bacteria and fungi

questions.q: Which bacterium changes milk into curd?
questions.why: Lactobacillus converts lactose into lactic acid, which sets the milk into curd.

questions.q: The antibiotic penicillin is obtained from:
questions.why: Penicillin is made by the mould Penicillium, discovered by Alexander Fleming.

questions.q: Which bacteria fix nitrogen in the root nodules of leguminous plants?
questions.why: Rhizobium lives in nodules of peas and beans and converts atmospheric nitrogen into compounds the plant can use.

questions.q: What does yeast do in bread making?
o: Adds vitamin C to the dough
Produces lactic acid that sours the dough
Produces carbon dioxide that makes the dough rise
questions.why: Yeast ferments sugars; the carbon dioxide gas forms bubbles that make the dough rise and the bread spongy.

questions.q: Which human disease is caused by a fungus?
questions.why: Ringworm is a fungal skin infection; cholera, tetanus and typhoid are bacterial.

long.q: State four useful activities of bacteria.
scheme: B1: Lactobacillus turns milk into curd and helps make cheese
B1: nitrogen-fixing bacteria such as Rhizobium increase soil fertility
B1: some bacteria (e.g. Streptomyces) give antibiotics such as streptomycin
B1: bacteria decompose dead matter and sewage, returning minerals to the soil (also retting of jute fibres or making vinegar)

long.q: Give two harmful activities of bacteria and two of fungi.
scheme: B1: bacteria cause diseases such as cholera, typhoid or tuberculosis
B1: bacteria spoil food (for example, milk turning sour, meat rotting)
B1: fungi cause plant diseases such as rust of wheat, or human diseases such as ringworm
B1: moulds spoil bread, fruit, leather and stored grain

long.q: Explain how each method preserves food: (a) salting or adding sugar; (b) refrigeration; (c) pasteurisation of milk.
scheme: B1: (a) strong salt or sugar draws water out of microbes by osmosis, so they cannot grow
B1: (b) low temperature slows the growth and enzyme activity of microbes
B1: (c) milk is heated to about 63 °C for 30 minutes (or 72 °C for 15 seconds) and cooled quickly, killing most harmful bacteria

long.q: Give reasons why bacteria and fungi that act as decomposers are called nature's scavengers.
scheme: B1: they break down dead bodies and wastes into simpler substances
B1: this cleans the environment and returns minerals to the soil for reuse

long.q: Describe in words how yeast reproduces by budding.
scheme: B1: a small outgrowth called a bud appears on the parent cell
B1: the nucleus divides and one daughter nucleus passes into the bud
B1: the bud grows and separates, or stays attached to form a chain of cells

questions.q: Deficiency of vitamin C causes:
questions.why: Scurvy shows as bleeding, spongy gums and slow healing of wounds; vitamin C comes from citrus fruits and amla.

questions.q: Which enzyme is present in saliva?
questions.why: Salivary amylase begins starch digestion in the mouth, changing starch to maltose.

questions.q: Bile is produced by the:
questions.why: The liver makes bile; the gall bladder only stores it until it is released into the duodenum.

questions.q: Where is most digested food absorbed?
questions.why: The ileum of the small intestine is long and lined with villi, giving a huge surface for absorption.

questions.q: Kwashiorkor in children is caused by a deficiency of:
questions.why: Kwashiorkor is protein deficiency; it shows as a swollen belly, thin limbs and swelling (oedema).

long.q: Name the enzyme and state its action: (a) the enzyme in gastric juice that acts on proteins; (b) the pancreatic enzyme that acts on proteins; (c) the pancreatic enzyme that acts on fats; (d) the intestinal enzyme that acts on maltose.
scheme: B1: (a) pepsin: converts proteins into peptones
B1: (b) trypsin: converts proteins and peptones into peptides
B1: (c) lipase: converts emulsified fats into fatty acids and glycerol
B1: (d) maltase: converts maltose into glucose

long.q: Give reasons: (a) hydrochloric acid is secreted in the stomach; (b) the inner wall of the small intestine has villi; (c) bile helps digestion although it contains no enzyme.
scheme: B1: (a) it makes the medium acidic so pepsin can act, and kills germs in the food
B1: (b) villi greatly increase the surface area for absorption of digested food
B1: (c) bile salts emulsify fats into tiny droplets, giving a larger surface for lipase to act on

long.q: What is a balanced diet? Why is roughage important in it?
scheme: B1: a balanced diet contains all the nutrients in the right amounts and proportions for the body's needs
B1: roughage (plant fibre, mainly cellulose) adds bulk to the food
B1: it helps the muscles of the intestine move food along (peristalsis) and prevents constipation

long.q: Describe in words the path of food through the human alimentary canal, naming each part and one thing that happens there.
scheme: B1: mouth (buccal cavity): food is chewed and mixed with saliva
B1: pharynx and oesophagus: food is swallowed and pushed down by peristalsis
B1: stomach: food is churned with gastric juice and protein digestion begins
B1: small intestine (duodenum and ileum): digestion is completed and food is absorbed into the blood
B1: large intestine: water is absorbed and undigested waste passes through the rectum and out of the anus

long.q: Name the deficiency disease and give one symptom when the diet lacks: (a) iodine; (b) vitamin A; (c) iron; (d) vitamin D.
scheme: B1: (a) goitre: swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck
B1: (b) night blindness: difficulty seeing in dim light
B1: (c) anaemia: tiredness and pale skin
B1: (d) rickets: soft, bent bones in children

questions.q: How many bones are there in the skeleton of an adult human?
questions.why: An adult has 206 bones; a newborn has about 300, some of which fuse during growth.

questions.q: Which is an example of a ball-and-socket joint?
o: Joints between the bones of the skull
questions.why: At the shoulder the round head of the humerus fits into a cup of the shoulder blade, allowing movement in all directions.

questions.q: Which is a hinge joint?
questions.why: A hinge joint allows movement in one plane only, like a door; the elbow and knee are hinge joints.

questions.q: Which tissue joins one bone to another at a joint?
questions.why: Ligaments are strong, slightly elastic bands holding the bones of a joint together.

questions.q: The fluid that lubricates a freely movable joint is:
questions.why: Synovial fluid in the joint cavity reduces friction between the cartilage-covered ends of bones.

long.q: State four functions of the human skeleton.
scheme: B1: support: it gives shape and a framework to the body
B1: protection: the skull protects the brain, and the ribs protect the heart and lungs
B1: movement: bones give attachment to muscles and act as levers
B1: red bone marrow makes blood cells (also bones store calcium and phosphorus)

long.q: Name the bone: (a) of the upper arm; (b) of the thigh; (c) that forms the knee cap; (d) of the lower jaw.
scheme: B1: (a) humerus
B1: (b) femur
B1: (c) patella
B1: (d) mandible

long.q: Describe in words the structure of a synovial joint.
scheme: B1: the ends of the bones are covered with smooth articular cartilage
B1: the joint is enclosed in a capsule lined by a synovial membrane
B1: the cavity is filled with synovial fluid, which lubricates the joint
B1: strong ligaments hold the bones in place

long.q: Explain how the biceps and triceps work as an antagonistic pair to bend and straighten the arm.
scheme: B1: muscles can only pull (contract); they cannot push
B1: to bend the elbow, the biceps contracts while the triceps relaxes
B1: to straighten the arm, the triceps contracts while the biceps relaxes

long.q: Distinguish between the axial and the appendicular skeleton, naming the bones in each.
scheme: B1: axial skeleton forms the main axis of the body: skull, vertebral column, ribs and sternum
B1: appendicular skeleton is made of the limbs and girdles: pectoral and pelvic girdles and the bones of arms and legs

questions.q: The outermost layer of the epidermis, made of dead flattened cells, is the:
questions.why: The cornified layer (stratum corneum) contains keratin and is constantly shed and replaced from below.

questions.q: Which pigment gives the skin its colour?
questions.why: Melanin, made in the Malpighian layer, gives colour and absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays.

questions.q: Sebaceous glands of the skin secrete:
questions.why: Sebum is an oily secretion that keeps the hair and skin soft and waterproof.

questions.q: In hot weather, the blood vessels in the dermis:
o: Widen (dilate) so that more heat is lost
questions.why: Vasodilation brings more warm blood close to the surface, so heat is lost by radiation.

questions.q: Which vitamin is made by the skin in sunlight?
questions.why: Ultraviolet light converts a substance in the skin into vitamin D, needed for healthy bones.

long.q: State four functions of the skin.
scheme: B1: protection against germs, injury and loss of water
B1: regulation of body temperature
B1: excretion of water, salts and a little urea in sweat
B1: sense organ for touch, pain, heat and cold (also makes vitamin D)

long.q: Describe in words how the skin helps to keep body temperature normal on a hot day.
scheme: B1: sweat glands secrete more sweat on to the skin surface
B1: evaporation of sweat takes latent heat from the body, cooling it
B1: capillaries in the dermis dilate, bringing more blood near the surface so more heat is lost

long.q: Describe in words how the skin helps to conserve heat on a cold day.
scheme: B1: capillaries in the dermis constrict, so less blood flows near the surface and less heat is lost
B1: sweating is reduced or stops
B1: hair erector muscles contract, raising the hairs (goose bumps); shivering of muscles also produces heat

long.q: Name the part of the skin that: (a) continually produces new cells of the epidermis; (b) stores fat and insulates the body; (c) contains blood vessels, sweat glands and sense receptors.
scheme: B1: (a) Malpighian (germinative) layer
B1: (b) subcutaneous fat (adipose) layer
B1: (c) dermis

long.q: Give reasons: (a) dark-skinned people are less likely to get sunburnt; (b) the skin does not let water in or out easily.
scheme: B1: (a) they have more melanin, which absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays
B1: (b) the cornified layer contains keratin and is coated with oily sebum, making it waterproof

questions.q: In which structures does exchange of gases take place in the lungs?
questions.why: The alveoli (air sacs) are thin-walled and surrounded by capillaries, so oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across easily.

questions.q: Which flap prevents food from entering the windpipe during swallowing?
questions.why: The epiglottis closes over the glottis when we swallow, guiding food into the oesophagus.

questions.q: During inhalation, the diaphragm:
questions.why: The contracting diaphragm flattens and moves down, increasing the volume of the chest cavity.

questions.q: The trachea does not collapse when air pressure in it falls because it has:
questions.why: Incomplete rings of cartilage keep the windpipe open at all times.

questions.q: Most oxygen is carried in the blood:
o: As oxyhaemoglobin in red blood cells
questions.why: Haemoglobin combines loosely with oxygen in the lungs to form oxyhaemoglobin and releases it in the tissues.

long.q: Describe in words the mechanism of inhalation (breathing in).
scheme: B1: the muscles of the diaphragm contract and the diaphragm flattens, moving downwards
B1: the external intercostal muscles contract, moving the ribs upwards and outwards
B1: the volume of the chest cavity increases, so the pressure inside the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure
B1: air rushes in through the nose and air passages into the lungs

long.q: Give reasons: (a) it is better to breathe through the nose than through the mouth; (b) state two ways in which alveoli are suited to gaseous exchange.
scheme: B1: (a) hairs and mucus in the nose trap dust and germs, and the air is warmed and moistened
B1: (b) alveoli have very thin walls (one cell thick) surrounded by a dense network of capillaries
B1: (b) they give a very large, moist surface area for diffusion

long.q: Define: (a) tidal volume; (b) vital capacity; (c) residual volume, giving an approximate value for each in an adult.
scheme: B1: (a) tidal volume: air breathed in or out in one normal breath, about 500 mL
B1: (b) vital capacity: the maximum air breathed out after the deepest breath in, about 3.5 to 4.5 litres
B1: (c) residual volume: air left in the lungs even after the strongest breath out, about 1.5 litres

long.q: Give three differences between breathing and respiration.
scheme: B1: breathing is a physical (mechanical) process of taking in and giving out air; respiration is the chemical oxidation of food
B1: breathing takes place in the lungs and air passages; respiration takes place in every living cell (in the mitochondria)
B1: breathing uses energy; respiration releases energy

long.q: State the approximate percentage of oxygen and of carbon dioxide in inhaled air and in exhaled air.
scheme: B1: inhaled air: oxygen about 21%
B1: exhaled air: oxygen about 16 to 17%
B1: inhaled air: carbon dioxide about 0.04%
B1: exhaled air: carbon dioxide about 4%

topics.name: Hygiene, diseases and aids to health

questions.q: Malaria is spread by the:
questions.why: The female Anopheles mosquito carries the Plasmodium parasite from one person to another when it sucks blood.

questions.q: Which disease is caused by a virus?
questions.why: Influenza (flu) is viral; cholera, typhoid and tuberculosis are caused by bacteria.

questions.q: The BCG vaccine protects against:
questions.why: BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guérin) is given to infants to protect against tuberculosis.

questions.q: Which is a water-borne disease?
questions.why: Cholera spreads through water and food contaminated with the faeces of infected people.

questions.q: Antibodies are produced by:
questions.why: Lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell, make antibodies that destroy specific germs.

long.q: Name the type of germ that causes each disease and state how it spreads: (a) tuberculosis; (b) dengue; (c) typhoid; (d) AIDS.
scheme: B1: (a) bacterium (Mycobacterium tuberculosis); spreads by droplets from coughing and sneezing
B1: (b) virus; spread by the bite of the Aedes mosquito
B1: (c) bacterium (Salmonella typhi); spreads through contaminated food and water
B1: (d) virus (HIV); spreads through unprotected sexual contact, infected blood or shared needles, and from mother to baby

long.q: Explain how vaccination protects a person against a disease.
scheme: B1: a vaccine contains dead or weakened germs, or their harmless products (toxoids)
B1: it makes the body produce antibodies and memory cells without causing the disease
B1: if the real germ enters later, antibodies are produced quickly and the germ is destroyed, so the person is immune

long.q: Suggest four measures to control the spread of malaria in a locality.
scheme: B1: drain stagnant water or cover water tanks so mosquitoes cannot breed
B1: spray kerosene oil or insecticide on water to kill larvae
B1: use mosquito nets, screens and repellents
B1: release larva-eating fish such as Gambusia into ponds, and treat patients promptly

long.q: Distinguish between communicable and non-communicable diseases, giving one example of each.
scheme: B1: communicable diseases are caused by germs and spread from one person to another, e.g. cholera
B1: non-communicable diseases do not spread from person to person, e.g. diabetes or cancer

long.q: Give reasons: (a) the housefly is called a carrier of disease; (b) a wound should be cleaned with an antiseptic.
scheme: B1: (a) it sits on filth and carries germs on its legs and body hairs to uncovered food
B1: (b) the antiseptic kills germs and prevents infection such as tetanus

questions.q: Which of these is biodegradable waste?
questions.why: Vegetable peels are broken down by microbes; plastics, glass and metals are not.

questions.q: Composting is:
o: Burning waste at a high temperature
Decomposition of organic waste by microbes into manure
questions.why: In composting, bacteria and fungi break down kitchen and garden waste into humus-rich manure.

questions.q: Which method of disposal reduces waste to ash by burning it at a high temperature?
questions.why: Incineration burns waste at high temperature, greatly reducing its volume.

questions.q: Used syringes and bandages from a hospital are best:
questions.why: Biomedical waste may carry germs, so it is destroyed at high temperature in an incinerator.

questions.q: Which is an example of reusing rather than recycling?
o: Melting old glass to make new bottles
Using an empty jam jar to store pulses
Pulping old newspapers into new paper
Melting old cans to make new ones
questions.why: Reuse means using an article again as it is; recycling means processing the material into new products.

long.q: Classify the following into biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste: paper, polythene, cow dung, DDT, dry leaves, glass.
scheme: B1: biodegradable: paper, cow dung, dry leaves
B1: non-biodegradable: polythene, DDT, glass

long.q: Describe in words how compost can be made from kitchen and garden waste.
scheme: B1: dig a pit or use a large container in a shaded place
B1: put in layers of kitchen and garden waste (no plastic, metal or glass), with layers of soil or cow dung
B1: keep it moist and turn it now and then to let air in
B1: in two to three months microbes (or earthworms, in vermicomposting) turn it into dark, crumbly manure

long.q: State three harmful effects of improper disposal of waste.
scheme: B1: heaps of garbage breed flies, mosquitoes and rats that spread disease
B1: rotting and burning waste pollutes the air with foul smells and smoke
B1: liquid seeping from dumps (leachate) pollutes soil and groundwater; plastics block drains and harm animals that eat them

long.q: Explain the terms: (a) sanitary landfill; (b) recycling; (c) e-waste.
scheme: B1: (a) a low-lying area where waste is dumped in layers and covered with soil
B1: (b) processing used materials such as paper, glass or metal into new products
B1: (c) discarded electrical and electronic goods such as old phones and computers

long.q: Give reasons: (a) plastic bags should not be burnt; (b) waste should be segregated at its source.
scheme: B1: (a) burning plastic releases toxic gases such as dioxins
B1: (b) it makes composting and recycling easier and reduces the waste sent to landfills

topics.name: Cell cycle, cell division and structure of chromosomes

questions.q: Mitosis in a body cell produces:
questions.why: Mitosis is equational division: each daughter cell gets the same number and kind of chromosomes as the parent.

questions.q: In which stage of mitosis do the chromosomes line up at the equator of the spindle?
questions.why: At metaphase each chromosome is attached by its centromere to spindle fibres on the equatorial plate.

questions.q: Meiosis takes place in cells of the:
questions.why: Meiosis forms gametes or spores, so it happens only in reproductive organs; the others divide by mitosis.

questions.q: The region where the two sister chromatids of a chromosome are held together is the:
questions.why: The centromere joins the two chromatids and is where spindle fibres attach.

questions.q: How many chromosomes are present in a human body (somatic) cell?
questions.why: Human somatic cells have 46 chromosomes (23 pairs); gametes have 23.

long.q: Give four differences between mitosis and meiosis.
scheme: B1: mitosis occurs in body (somatic) cells; meiosis occurs in reproductive cells of the gonads
B1: mitosis involves one division; meiosis involves two successive divisions
B1: mitosis produces two daughter cells; meiosis produces four
B1: in mitosis the chromosome number stays the same (diploid); in meiosis it is halved (haploid)

long.q: Describe in words the events of anaphase and telophase of mitosis in an animal cell.
scheme: B1: anaphase: the centromere of each chromosome splits and the sister chromatids separate
B1: the chromatids (now daughter chromosomes) are pulled to opposite poles by the spindle fibres
B1: telophase: chromosomes reach the poles and uncoil; the nuclear membrane and nucleolus reappear around each set
B1: the cytoplasm divides by a furrow that deepens from the outside inwards (cytokinesis)

long.q: Explain how cytokinesis in a plant cell differs from that in an animal cell.
scheme: B1: in an animal cell a furrow forms in the cell membrane and deepens inwards until the cell is pinched into two
B1: in a plant cell a cell plate forms in the middle and grows outwards to the walls, because the rigid wall cannot furrow

long.q: Define: (a) gene; (b) chromatin; (c) homologous chromosomes.
scheme: B1: (a) a segment of DNA that carries the information for one characteristic
B1: (b) the thread-like network of DNA and protein seen in the nucleus of a non-dividing cell
B1: (c) a pair of chromosomes alike in size and shape, one from each parent, carrying genes for the same characters

long.q: Give reasons: (a) meiosis is called reduction division; (b) state two reasons why meiosis is important.
scheme: B1: (a) the chromosome number is halved, from diploid in the parent cell to haploid in the gametes
B1: (b) it keeps the chromosome number constant from generation to generation when gametes fuse at fertilisation
B1: (b) crossing over and random sorting of chromosomes produce variation in the offspring

questions.q: A pure tall pea plant (TT) is crossed with a pure dwarf plant (tt). The F1 plants are:
questions.why: Every F1 plant is Tt, and tall is dominant over dwarf.

questions.q: The phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation of a monohybrid cross is:
questions.why: Tt × Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt and tt; three show the dominant trait and one the recessive. 1 : 2 : 1 is the genotypic ratio.

questions.q: Alternative forms of the same gene, such as T and t, are called:
questions.why: Alleles occupy the same position on homologous chromosomes and control the same character.

questions.q: Red-green colour blindness in humans is:
o: Carried on the Y chromosome only
questions.why: The gene is recessive and lies on the X chromosome, so it is much commoner in males, who have only one X.

questions.q: The sex of a human child is decided by:
o: Whether the father's sperm carries an X or a Y chromosome
questions.why: Every egg carries an X; a sperm carries X (girl) or Y (boy).

long.q: A pure tall pea plant (TT) is crossed with a pure dwarf plant (tt). Work out the genotype and phenotype of the F1, and the genotypic and phenotypic ratios of the F2 obtained by selfing the F1.
scheme: B1: gametes of the parents are T and t
B1: F1 genotype Tt; all plants tall
B1: F1 plants form gametes T and t in equal numbers
B1: F2 genotypic ratio TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1
B1: F2 phenotypic ratio 3 tall : 1 dwarf
long.ans: F1 all Tt (tall); F2 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, 3 tall : 1 dwarf

long.q: State Mendel's law of segregation and law of independent assortment.
scheme: B1: segregation: the two alleles of a gene separate when gametes form, so each gamete carries only one allele
B1: independent assortment: alleles of different genes sort into gametes independently of one another

long.q: Define: (a) genotype; (b) phenotype; (c) homozygous; (d) heterozygous.
scheme: B1: (a) the genetic make-up of an organism for a character, e.g. Tt
B1: (b) the visible (observable) characteristic, e.g. tall
B1: (c) having two identical alleles for a character, e.g. TT or tt
B1: (d) having two different alleles for a character, e.g. Tt

long.q: A pea plant with round yellow seeds (RRYY) is crossed with one having wrinkled green seeds (rryy). State the genotype and phenotype of the F1 and the phenotypic ratio of the F2.
scheme: B1: F1 genotype RrYy; all round yellow
B1: F2 phenotypes: round yellow, round green, wrinkled yellow, wrinkled green
B1: in the ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1

long.q: Explain why a colour-blind father cannot pass colour blindness to his son.
scheme: B1: the colour-blindness gene is carried on the X chromosome
B1: a son receives his X chromosome from his mother and his Y chromosome from his father
B1: so the father's X, carrying the gene, goes only to his daughters (who become carriers)

questions.q: The movement of water from a dilute solution to a more concentrated one through a semi-permeable membrane is:
questions.why: Osmosis is the movement of water (solvent) across a semi-permeable membrane from higher to lower water concentration.

questions.q: A plant cell shows plasmolysis when placed in:
questions.why: Water leaves the cell by exosmosis and the cytoplasm shrinks away from the cell wall.

questions.q: Root hairs take in water mainly by:
questions.why: The cell sap of a root hair is more concentrated than soil water, so water enters by osmosis.

questions.q: Dry seeds swell when soaked in water because of:
questions.why: Imbibition is the absorption of water by solid substances such as cellulose and starch, causing swelling.

questions.q: Water oozing from the cut stump of a well-watered plant shows the existence of:
questions.why: Root pressure, built up by root cells, pushes water up the xylem even without leaves.

long.q: Explain how water passes from the soil into the xylem of a root.
scheme: B1: the cell sap of the root hair is more concentrated than the soil water
B1: water enters the root hair by osmosis through its cell wall and membrane
B1: water passes from cell to cell across the cortex by osmosis, each cell being more concentrated than the one before
B1: it crosses the endodermis and pericycle into the xylem, and is pushed up by root pressure

long.q: State three ways in which root hairs are suited to absorbing water.
scheme: B1: they are long, thin and numerous, giving a very large surface area
B1: their walls are thin, so water passes in easily
B1: they have concentrated cell sap in a large vacuole, so water enters by osmosis

long.q: Give three differences between diffusion and osmosis.
scheme: B1: diffusion can involve solids, liquids or gases; osmosis involves only the solvent, water
B1: diffusion does not need a membrane; osmosis needs a semi-permeable membrane
B1: in diffusion a substance moves from its higher to its lower concentration; in osmosis water moves from the dilute to the concentrated solution

long.q: Describe in words an experiment using a potato osmometer to demonstrate osmosis.
scheme: B1: a peeled potato is hollowed into a cup and placed in a beaker of water
B1: strong sugar solution is poured into the cavity and its level marked with a pin
B1: after a few hours the level of the sugar solution rises
B1: water has entered from the beaker through the living potato cells (acting as a semi-permeable membrane) by osmosis; a boiled potato shows no rise

long.q: Give reasons: (a) adding too much fertiliser to soil can make plants wilt; (b) raw mango pieces shrivel when salted.
scheme: B1: (a) the soil solution becomes more concentrated than the cell sap, so water leaves the root cells by exosmosis
B1: (b) water leaves the mango cells by exosmosis into the strong salt solution, so the cells are plasmolysed

questions.q: Most of the water lost by transpiration passes out through the:
questions.why: Stomatal transpiration accounts for about 90% of the water lost; cuticle and lenticels lose much less.

questions.q: The rate of transpiration increases when there is:
questions.why: Wind removes humid air round the leaf and warmth speeds evaporation, so water vapour diffuses out faster.

questions.q: Which instrument measures the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot?
questions.why: In a potometer the movement of an air bubble along a capillary shows how fast the shoot takes up water.

questions.q: Dry cobalt chloride paper changes colour in the presence of water from:
questions.why: Anhydrous cobalt chloride is blue; it turns pink when it absorbs water.

questions.q: Loss of water as liquid droplets from the leaf margins of grasses in the early morning is:
questions.why: Guttation occurs through hydathodes when root pressure is high and transpiration is low.

long.q: State three ways in which transpiration is useful to a plant.
scheme: B1: it creates a suction force (transpiration pull) that draws water and minerals up the xylem
B1: evaporation of water cools the leaves in hot weather
B1: it helps distribute the minerals dissolved in the water to all parts of the plant

long.q: Describe in words an experiment with cobalt chloride paper to show that the lower surface of a leaf loses more water than the upper surface.
scheme: B1: place a dry blue cobalt chloride paper on each surface of a leaf of a well-watered potted plant
B1: hold the papers in place with glass slides and a clip
B1: the paper on the lower surface turns pink sooner than the paper on the upper surface
B1: the lower surface of a dicot leaf has more stomata, so it transpires more

long.q: Explain how a stoma opens.
scheme: B1: the guard cells take in water from neighbouring cells and become turgid (as potassium ions and sugars build up in them)
B1: the inner wall of each guard cell is thick and inelastic while the outer wall is thin and elastic
B1: so the turgid guard cells bend outwards and the pore between them opens

long.q: State three adaptations of desert plants that reduce transpiration.
scheme: B1: leaves reduced to spines (as in cactus) to cut down the surface area
B1: thick waxy cuticle on the surface
B1: few or sunken stomata, which open only at night

long.q: Give reasons: (a) some leaves are removed from a seedling when it is transplanted; (b) transpiration is called a necessary evil.
scheme: B1: (a) the roots are damaged and absorb less water, so reducing the leaves cuts water loss and prevents wilting
B1: (b) it is necessary for the transpiration pull and cooling, but it wastes a lot of water and may cause wilting

questions.q: The oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from:
questions.why: Water is split by light energy (photolysis), releasing oxygen.

questions.q: The light reaction of photosynthesis takes place in the:
questions.why: The grana (stacks of thylakoids) contain chlorophyll, which traps light; the dark reaction takes place in the stroma.

questions.q: Which reagent is used to test a leaf for starch?
questions.why: Iodine turns blue-black where starch is present.

questions.q: Before a starch-test experiment, a potted plant is destarched by:
o: Keeping it in the dark for 24 to 48 hours
questions.why: In darkness the plant cannot photosynthesise and uses up its stored starch, so any starch found later was made during the experiment.

questions.q: During the starch test, a leaf is boiled in alcohol to:
questions.why: Alcohol dissolves the chlorophyll, so the colour change with iodine can be seen clearly. Boiling in water kills and softens the leaf.

long.q: Write the balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis, stating the conditions.
scheme: B1: 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O (correctly balanced)
B1: conditions: sunlight and chlorophyll

long.q: Describe in words an experiment to show that carbon dioxide is necessary for photosynthesis.
scheme: B1: destarch a potted plant by keeping it in the dark for two days
B1: insert half of one leaf into a wide-mouthed bottle containing potassium hydroxide solution (which absorbs carbon dioxide), through a split cork sealed with grease
B1: keep the plant in sunlight for several hours
B1: remove the leaf and test it for starch (boil in water, then alcohol, then add iodine)
B1: the part inside the bottle stays brown (no starch) while the part outside turns blue-black, so carbon dioxide is needed

long.q: Give four differences between the light and dark reactions of photosynthesis.
scheme: B1: the light reaction occurs in the grana; the dark reaction in the stroma
B1: the light reaction needs light; the dark reaction does not need light directly
B1: in the light reaction water is split (photolysis) and oxygen is released
B1: in the dark reaction carbon dioxide is reduced to glucose using ATP and NADPH from the light reaction

long.q: State four ways in which a leaf is adapted for photosynthesis.
scheme: B1: broad, flat lamina to absorb maximum light
B1: thin, so carbon dioxide diffuses quickly to all cells
B1: many stomata for gaseous exchange
B1: palisade cells packed with chloroplasts near the upper surface, and veins that bring water and remove food

long.q: Give reasons: (a) a water plant gives off bubbles of gas faster in bright light; (b) raising the carbon dioxide concentration increases the rate of photosynthesis only up to a limit; (c) photosynthesis is essential for animal life.
scheme: B1: (a) bright light increases the rate of photosynthesis, so more oxygen is released
B1: (b) carbon dioxide is a raw material, but beyond a point another factor such as light or temperature limits the rate
B1: (c) it provides the food (directly or through food chains) and the oxygen that animals need

questions.q: Which plant hormone causes cell elongation and is responsible for phototropism?
questions.why: Auxin made at the shoot tip collects on the shaded side and makes those cells grow longer.

questions.q: Which plant hormone is a gas that speeds up fruit ripening?
questions.why: Ethylene gas is released by ripening fruits and hastens ripening of nearby fruits.

questions.q: Which hormone causes stomata to close and seeds to stay dormant in stress conditions?
questions.why: Abscisic acid (ABA), the stress hormone, inhibits growth and closes stomata during water shortage.

questions.q: Roots growing downwards in the direction of gravity show:
questions.why: Growth towards gravity is positive geotropism; shoots show negative geotropism.

questions.q: Gibberellins are used to:
o: Make stems lengthen and break seed dormancy
questions.why: Gibberellins cause stem elongation (even in dwarf varieties) and help seeds to germinate.

long.q: Name the plant hormone that: (a) promotes cell division; (b) makes a genetically dwarf plant grow tall; (c) promotes leaf fall and dormancy; (d) is used, in a synthetic form, as a weedkiller.
scheme: B1: (a) cytokinin
B1: (b) gibberellin
B1: (c) abscisic acid
B1: (d) auxin (e.g. 2,4-D)

long.q: Explain how auxin causes a shoot to bend towards light coming from one side.
scheme: B1: auxin is made at the tip of the shoot
B1: it moves away from the lit side and collects on the shaded side
B1: cells on the shaded side elongate more, so the shoot bends towards the light

long.q: Define the following tropic movements and give one example of each: (a) hydrotropism; (b) thigmotropism; (c) chemotropism.
scheme: B1: (a) growth movement in response to water, e.g. roots growing towards moist soil
B1: (b) growth movement in response to touch, e.g. tendrils of a pea coiling round a support
B1: (c) growth movement in response to chemicals, e.g. the pollen tube growing towards the ovule

long.q: Describe in words an experiment to show geotropism in germinating seeds.
scheme: B1: pin soaked or germinating seeds, with their radicles pointing in different directions, on moist blotting paper or cork inside a box
B1: keep the box in the dark, so light has no effect, for a few days
B1: all radicles bend and grow downwards while the plumules grow upwards
B1: so roots are positively and shoots negatively geotropic

long.q: State three practical uses of plant hormones in agriculture or horticulture.
scheme: B1: auxins help stem cuttings to form roots
B1: ethylene is used to ripen fruits such as bananas and mangoes evenly
B1: gibberellins increase the size of grapes or produce seedless fruits (cytokinins keep cut flowers and leaves fresh longer)

questions.q: Which blood vessel carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart?
questions.why: Pulmonary veins are the only veins carrying oxygenated blood; they open into the left atrium.

questions.q: The valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle is the:
questions.why: The bicuspid valve has two flaps; the tricuspid lies on the right side of the heart.

questions.q: Which blood group is called the universal donor?
questions.why: Group O red cells carry no A or B antigens, so they are not clumped by the recipient's antibodies.

questions.q: The normal blood pressure of a healthy adult is about:
questions.why: Systolic pressure is about 120 mm Hg and diastolic about 80 mm Hg.

questions.q: The pacemaker of the human heart is the:
questions.why: The SA node in the wall of the right atrium starts each heartbeat.

long.q: Give four differences between arteries and veins.
scheme: B1: arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry blood towards the heart
B1: arteries have thick, muscular, elastic walls; veins have thinner walls and a wider lumen
B1: arteries have no valves (except at their origin); veins have valves along their length
B1: blood in arteries is under high pressure and flows in spurts; in veins it is under low pressure and flows smoothly

long.q: Trace the path of blood through the human heart and body in double circulation, starting from the right atrium.
scheme: B1: right atrium → (through the tricuspid valve) → right ventricle
B1: right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs, where the blood is oxygenated
B1: lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → (through the bicuspid valve) → left ventricle
B1: left ventricle → aorta → arteries to all body organs (systemic circulation)
B1: deoxygenated blood returns through the venae cavae to the right atrium, so blood passes through the heart twice in one round

long.q: Give reasons: (a) the wall of the left ventricle is thicker than that of the right ventricle; (b) mammalian red blood cells have no nucleus; (c) veins have valves.
scheme: B1: (a) the left ventricle pumps blood to the whole body at high pressure; the right pumps only to the lungs
B1: (b) there is more room for haemoglobin, so each cell carries more oxygen
B1: (c) valves prevent blood, which is under low pressure, from flowing backwards

long.q: Name: (a) the blood cells that help in clotting; (b) the white blood cells that engulf germs; (c) the plasma protein that forms fibrin; (d) the fluid that drains from the tissues into lymph vessels.
scheme: B1: (a) platelets (thrombocytes)
B1: (b) neutrophils (phagocytes)
B1: (c) fibrinogen
B1: (d) lymph

long.q: Describe in words how blood clots at a wound.
scheme: B1: damaged tissues and platelets release thromboplastin (thrombokinase)
B1: in the presence of calcium ions, thromboplastin changes prothrombin into thrombin
B1: thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads
B1: the fibrin threads form a mesh that traps blood cells, forming a clot that seals the wound

questions.q: The structural and functional unit of the kidney is the:
questions.why: Each kidney has about a million nephrons, which filter blood and form urine.

questions.q: Which tube carries urine from the kidney to the urinary bladder?
questions.why: The ureter leads from the pelvis of the kidney to the bladder; the urethra leads from the bladder to the outside.

questions.q: Ultrafiltration of blood takes place in the:
questions.why: Blood under high pressure in the glomerulus is filtered into the Bowman's capsule.

questions.q: Which substance is NOT normally present in the urine of a healthy person?
questions.why: All glucose in the filtrate is reabsorbed by the tubules; glucose in urine suggests diabetes.

questions.q: ADH (antidiuretic hormone) acts on the kidney tubules to:
questions.why: ADH makes the tubules reabsorb more water, so less, more concentrated urine is produced.

long.q: Describe in words the three main steps in the formation of urine.
scheme: B1: ultrafiltration: blood under high pressure in the glomerulus is filtered into the Bowman's capsule (the afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent)
B1: selective reabsorption: glucose, useful salts and much water are taken back into the blood from the tubules
B1: tubular secretion: extra substances such as potassium ions, hydrogen ions and creatinine are passed from the blood into the tubule

long.q: Name the main excretory product removed by each organ: (a) lungs; (b) skin; (c) kidneys; (d) liver.
scheme: B1: (a) carbon dioxide and water vapour
B1: (b) sweat (water, salts and a little urea)
B1: (c) urea, in urine
B1: (d) bile pigments

long.q: Give reasons: (a) the afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole; (b) we pass more urine in winter than in summer.
scheme: B1: (a) this builds up high pressure in the glomerulus, needed for ultrafiltration
B1: (b) we sweat less in winter, so more water is removed by the kidneys

long.q: Describe in words the structure of a nephron.
scheme: B1: Bowman's capsule: a double-walled cup at the start of the nephron
B1: glomerulus: a knot of capillaries inside the capsule, supplied by the afferent arteriole
B1: proximal convoluted tubule leading from the capsule
B1: U-shaped loop of Henle followed by the distal convoluted tubule
B1: which opens into a collecting duct that leads to the pelvis of the kidney

long.q: What is osmoregulation? Explain how the kidneys carry it out.
scheme: B1: osmoregulation is keeping the water and salt balance of the blood constant
B1: when the body is short of water, more ADH is released, more water is reabsorbed and a small volume of concentrated urine is passed
B1: when there is excess water, less ADH is released and a large volume of dilute urine is passed

questions.q: Which part of the brain maintains balance and coordinates voluntary movements?
questions.why: The cerebellum keeps posture and balance and makes movements smooth and precise.

questions.q: Which part of the brain controls involuntary actions such as heartbeat and breathing?
questions.why: The medulla oblongata contains the centres for heartbeat, breathing, swallowing and coughing.

questions.q: The junction between two neurons, across which an impulse passes chemically, is the:
questions.why: At a synapse a chemical transmitter carries the impulse across a tiny gap.

questions.q: Pulling the hand away from a hot object is a reflex action controlled by the:
questions.why: The spinal cord links sensory and motor neurons directly, so the response is quick, before the brain is aware.

questions.q: The protective membranes covering the brain and spinal cord are the:
questions.why: The three meninges protect the central nervous system; pleura cover the lungs.

long.q: Describe in words the path of a reflex arc when the hand touches a hot object.
scheme: B1: receptors in the skin detect the heat
B1: a sensory (afferent) neuron carries the impulse to the spinal cord
B1: a relay (intermediate) neuron in the grey matter of the spinal cord passes it on
B1: a motor (efferent) neuron carries the impulse to the effector
B1: the effector muscle contracts and the hand is withdrawn, before the brain becomes aware of the pain

long.q: Name the part of the brain responsible for: (a) thinking, memory and intelligence; (b) control of hunger, thirst and body temperature; (c) relaying sensory impulses to the cerebrum.
scheme: B1: (a) cerebrum
B1: (b) hypothalamus
B1: (c) thalamus

long.q: Give three differences between a reflex action and a voluntary action.
scheme: B1: a reflex is automatic, without conscious will; a voluntary action is done consciously
B1: a reflex is mostly controlled by the spinal cord; a voluntary action by the cerebrum
B1: a reflex is very quick and protective; a voluntary action is slower

long.q: What is a conditioned reflex? Give an example.
scheme: B1: a reflex that is learnt through experience or training, not inborn
B1: example: the mouth watering at the smell of a favourite food, or a trained cyclist balancing without thinking

long.q: Give reasons: (a) an injury to the spinal cord in the neck can paralyse the body below it; (b) cerebrospinal fluid is important; (c) state how the arrangement of grey and white matter in the cerebrum differs from that in the spinal cord.
scheme: B1: (a) impulses can no longer pass between the brain and the parts below the injury
B1: (b) it cushions the brain and spinal cord against shocks and supplies them with nutrients
B1: (c) in the cerebrum grey matter is outside and white matter inside; in the spinal cord grey matter is inside and white matter outside

topics.name: Sense organs: the eye and the ear

questions.q: The light-sensitive layer of the eye is the:
questions.why: The retina contains rods and cones, which convert light into nerve impulses.

questions.q: The blind spot cannot form an image because it has no:
questions.why: The blind spot is where the optic nerve leaves the eye; it lacks photoreceptors.

questions.q: Myopia (short sight) is corrected by spectacles with:
questions.why: In myopia the image forms in front of the retina; a diverging concave lens moves it back on to the retina.

questions.q: Which part of the ear helps to maintain balance?
questions.why: Fluid moving in the semicircular canals signals rotation of the head to the brain.

questions.q: The Eustachian tube connects the:
o: Outer ear and the middle ear
questions.why: It keeps the air pressure on both sides of the eardrum equal.

long.q: Explain how the eye focuses on a near object (accommodation).
scheme: B1: the ciliary muscles contract
B1: the suspensory ligaments become slack
B1: the lens becomes thicker (more convex), its focal length decreases and the image is focused on the retina

long.q: Name the defect and how it is corrected: (a) distant objects look blurred because the image forms in front of the retina; (b) near objects look blurred because the image forms behind the retina; (c) the cornea has uneven curvature; (d) the lens becomes cloudy in old age.
scheme: B1: (a) myopia: concave (diverging) lens
B1: (b) hypermetropia: convex (converging) lens
B1: (c) astigmatism: cylindrical lens
B1: (d) cataract: surgery to replace the lens with an artificial one

long.q: Trace the path of sound waves from the pinna to the brain.
scheme: B1: the pinna collects sound, which passes along the ear canal and makes the eardrum (tympanum) vibrate
B1: the ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) carry and amplify the vibrations
B1: the stapes vibrates the oval window, setting up waves in the fluid of the cochlea
B1: sensory hair cells in the organ of Corti are stimulated
B1: impulses travel along the auditory nerve to the hearing centre of the cerebrum

long.q: Give two differences between rods and cones.
scheme: B1: rods work in dim light and do not detect colour; they contain rhodopsin
B1: cones work in bright light and detect colour; they contain iodopsin

long.q: Give reasons: (a) we cannot see clearly for a while on entering a dark room from bright sunlight; (b) we swallow when our ears feel blocked in an aircraft taking off; (c) the pupil becomes smaller in bright light.
scheme: B1: (a) rhodopsin in the rods, bleached by bright light, takes time to re-form, and the pupil takes time to widen
B1: (b) swallowing opens the Eustachian tube and equalises the air pressure on both sides of the eardrum
B1: (c) the circular muscles of the iris contract, reducing the light entering and protecting the retina

questions.q: Which gland is called the master gland?
questions.why: The pituitary secretes hormones that control several other endocrine glands.

questions.q: Insulin is secreted by the:
o: Beta cells of the islets of Langerhans
Alpha cells of the islets of Langerhans
questions.why: Beta cells make insulin, which lowers blood sugar; alpha cells make glucagon, which raises it.

questions.q: Iodine is needed by the body to make:
questions.why: Thyroxine contains iodine; its lack causes goitre.

questions.q: Which hormone prepares the body for 'fight or flight'?
questions.why: Adrenaline from the adrenal medulla raises the heart rate, blood sugar and breathing rate in emergencies.

questions.q: Excess growth hormone in childhood causes:
questions.why: Too much growth hormone before the bones stop growing produces abnormal height.

long.q: Give two differences between endocrine and exocrine glands.
scheme: B1: endocrine glands are ductless and pour their secretions (hormones) directly into the blood
B1: exocrine glands have ducts that carry secretions to a surface or cavity, e.g. salivary glands

long.q: Name the hormone and the gland that secretes it: (a) lowers blood sugar; (b) controls the basal metabolic rate; (c) increases the heartbeat in danger; (d) increases reabsorption of water in the kidney.
scheme: B1: (a) insulin: pancreas (islets of Langerhans)
B1: (b) thyroxine: thyroid
B1: (c) adrenaline: adrenal medulla
B1: (d) ADH (vasopressin): pituitary

long.q: Name the disorder caused by: (a) too little insulin; (b) too little thyroxine in a child; (c) lack of iodine in the diet; (d) too little ADH.
scheme: B1: (a) diabetes mellitus
B1: (b) cretinism
B1: (c) simple goitre
B1: (d) diabetes insipidus
long.ans: diabetes mellitus; cretinism; goitre; diabetes insipidus

long.q: Explain why the pancreas is both an exocrine and an endocrine gland.
scheme: B1: its exocrine part secretes pancreatic juice containing enzymes through a duct into the duodenum
B1: its islets of Langerhans secrete insulin and glucagon directly into the blood

long.q: Give three differences between hormonal (chemical) and nervous coordination.
scheme: B1: hormones are chemicals carried by the blood; nervous messages are electrical impulses carried by neurons
B1: hormonal action is slower but longer-lasting; nervous action is fast and brief
B1: hormones may act on many organs throughout the body; nerve impulses reach a precise muscle or gland

questions.q: In humans, fertilisation normally takes place in the:
questions.why: The egg meets the sperm in the upper part of the oviduct; the zygote then moves to the uterus.

questions.q: Sperms are produced in the:
questions.why: Sperms form in the seminiferous tubules and are stored and matured in the epididymis.

questions.q: The embryo becomes embedded (implanted) in the:
questions.why: The thick, blood-rich endometrium receives the embryo, and the placenta forms there.

questions.q: In a regular 28-day menstrual cycle, ovulation usually occurs around day:
questions.why: The egg is released about midway through the cycle, roughly 14 days before the next menstruation.

questions.q: Which hormone, secreted by the corpus luteum and later the placenta, maintains pregnancy?
questions.why: Progesterone keeps the uterine lining thick and prevents further ovulation.

long.q: State the function of: (a) the scrotum; (b) the epididymis; (c) the vas deferens; (d) the seminal vesicles and prostate gland.
scheme: B1: (a) holds the testes outside the body at a temperature 2 to 3 °C lower than body temperature, needed for sperm formation
B1: (b) stores sperms and lets them mature
B1: (c) carries sperms from the epididymis to the urethra
B1: (d) secrete fluids that nourish the sperms and help them swim

long.q: Describe in words the main events of the menstrual cycle.
scheme: B1: menstruation (about days 1 to 5): the uterine lining breaks down and is shed with blood
B1: FSH from the pituitary makes a follicle grow; oestrogen from it rebuilds the uterine lining
B1: ovulation about day 14, after a surge of LH, releases an egg from the ovary
B1: the empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone to keep the lining ready; without fertilisation it breaks down and the cycle repeats

long.q: State three functions of the placenta.
scheme: B1: food and oxygen pass from the mother's blood into the foetus's blood
B1: carbon dioxide and urea pass from the foetus to the mother for removal
B1: it secretes hormones such as progesterone (and acts as a barrier to some germs)

long.q: Define: (a) puberty; (b) menopause; (c) gestation period.
scheme: B1: (a) the age (about 10 to 14 years) at which reproductive organs mature and secondary sexual characters appear
B1: (b) the permanent stopping of ovulation and menstruation in women, usually around 45 to 50 years
B1: (c) the time from fertilisation to birth, about 280 days (nine months) in humans

long.q: Give reasons: (a) identical twins are always of the same sex; (b) the foetus is surrounded by amniotic fluid.
scheme: B1: (a) they develop from a single zygote that splits into two, so they have the same genes and sex chromosomes
B1: (b) the fluid protects the foetus from shocks and keeps its temperature steady

questions.q: The theory of natural selection was put forward by:
questions.why: Darwin explained evolution by natural selection, published in 1859; Lamarck proposed inheritance of acquired characters.

questions.q: Organs that have the same basic structure and origin but different functions, such as the forelimbs of a human, whale and bat, are:
questions.why: Homologous organs share a common plan because they come from a common ancestor.

questions.q: Which of these is a vestigial organ in humans?
questions.why: The appendix is reduced and has no clear digestive role in humans, but is functional in some plant-eating mammals.

questions.q: Lamarck's theory of evolution is based on:
questions.why: Lamarck held that changes acquired by use or disuse during life are passed on to offspring.

questions.q: The wings of a bird and the wings of an insect are:
questions.why: They do the same job (flying) but are built differently and have different origins.

long.q: State four main points of Darwin's theory of natural selection.
scheme: B1: organisms produce far more offspring than can survive (overproduction)
B1: there is a struggle for existence for limited food and space
B1: individuals vary, and some variations are more useful than others
B1: those with useful variations survive and reproduce (survival of the fittest) and pass them on, so over many generations new species arise

long.q: Explain how fossils provide evidence for evolution.
scheme: B1: fossils are remains or impressions of organisms of the past preserved in rocks, and the age of the rocks can be found
B1: older rocks contain simpler forms and younger rocks more complex ones, showing gradual change; links such as Archaeopteryx show features of two groups

long.q: Name, with one example each: (a) homologous organs; (b) analogous organs; (c) a vestigial organ in humans.
scheme: B1: (a) forelimbs of a human, whale and bat
B1: (b) wings of a bird and of an insect
B1: (c) vermiform appendix, nictitating membrane or ear muscles

long.q: State three features in which modern humans differ from apes.
scheme: B1: a much larger brain, about 1350 to 1450 cm³
B1: fully erect posture and walking on two legs
B1: a well-developed opposable thumb for precise grip, smaller jaws with a chin, and the power of speech

long.q: Explain how Lamarck accounted for the long neck of the giraffe, and why his theory is rejected.
scheme: B1: ancestors of giraffes stretched their necks to reach leaves high on trees
B1: the slightly longer necks acquired in this way were passed on, and over generations the neck became long
B1: it is rejected because characters acquired during life, such as muscles built by exercise, are not inherited (Weismann cut the tails of mice for many generations, yet tails did not shorten)

questions.q: Population explosion means a rapid rise in population because:
o: The birth rate stays high while the death rate falls
Birth rate and death rate are equal
questions.why: Better medicine lowers deaths, but if births remain high the gap makes the population grow very fast.

questions.q: In India, a census is held every:
questions.why: India has normally counted its population once every ten years.

questions.q: Which is a permanent method of birth control for men?
questions.why: In vasectomy the vasa deferentia are cut and tied; tubectomy is the equivalent operation for women.

questions.q: The term natality means:
questions.why: Natality is the number of live births per thousand people per year.

questions.q: A Copper-T is a:
questions.why: A Copper-T is placed in the uterus by a doctor and prevents implantation.

long.q: State three causes of the rapid growth of population in India.
scheme: B1: better medical care and vaccination have lowered the death rate and infant mortality
B1: the birth rate has remained high
B1: because of early marriage, illiteracy and lack of awareness of family planning (or the wish for a son)

long.q: State three effects of a population explosion.
scheme: B1: shortage of food, water and housing
B1: unemployment and poverty
B1: pressure on resources, leading to deforestation and pollution

long.q: Define: (a) population density; (b) birth rate; (c) death rate.
scheme: B1: (a) the number of people living per square kilometre of land
B1: (b) the number of live births per 1000 people in a year
B1: (c) the number of deaths per 1000 people in a year

long.q: A town had 50,000 people at the start of a year. During the year there were 1,500 births and 500 deaths. Ignoring migration, calculate the birth rate, the death rate (both per 1000) and the growth rate as a percentage.
scheme: A1: growth rate = (30 − 10) per 1000 = 2%

long.q: Name one method of family planning in each category: (a) barrier; (b) chemical (hormonal); (c) intrauterine device; (d) surgical.
scheme: B1: (a) condom or diaphragm
B1: (b) oral contraceptive pill
B1: (c) Copper-T
B1: (d) vasectomy or tubectomy

questions.q: Which pollutants are mainly responsible for the thinning of the ozone layer?
questions.why: CFCs from old refrigerators and aerosols release chlorine, which breaks down ozone in the upper atmosphere.

questions.q: Acid rain is caused mainly by:
questions.why: These gases dissolve in rainwater to form sulphuric and nitric acids.

questions.q: Which greenhouse gas is given off by paddy fields and cattle?
questions.why: Bacteria in waterlogged paddy fields and in the stomachs of cattle produce methane.

questions.q: The loudness of sound is measured in:
questions.why: Decibels (dB) measure sound level; sounds above about 80 dB can damage hearing over time.

questions.q: In a lake polluted by DDT, the highest concentration of DDT is found in:
questions.why: DDT is not broken down and builds up at each step of the food chain (biomagnification), so top consumers have the most.

long.q: Give one source and one harmful effect of each air pollutant: (a) carbon monoxide; (b) sulphur dioxide; (c) suspended particulate matter.
scheme: B1: (a) exhaust of petrol and diesel vehicles; it combines with haemoglobin and reduces the oxygen carried by blood
B1: (b) burning coal in thermal power plants; it causes acid rain and breathing problems
B1: (c) smoke, dust from construction and burning of crop residue; it causes lung diseases such as asthma

long.q: Explain the greenhouse effect and how it leads to global warming.
scheme: B1: sunlight (short-wave radiation) passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface
B1: the Earth gives out long-wave infrared radiation
B1: greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, methane and CFCs absorb this heat and trap it in the atmosphere
B1: burning fossil fuels and cutting forests increase these gases, raising the Earth's average temperature (global warming), which melts ice and raises sea level

long.q: Give two causes of water pollution and two measures to control it.
scheme: B1: untreated sewage discharged into rivers
B1: industrial effluents containing harmful chemicals, or runoff of fertilisers and pesticides from fields
B1: treat sewage and industrial waste before it is released
B1: use fertilisers and pesticides carefully and avoid bathing animals or washing clothes in drinking-water sources

long.q: Give reasons: (a) the marble of old monuments such as the Taj Mahal is turning yellow and pitted; (b) fish die in a lake into which fertiliser-rich water drains; (c) radioactive pollution is very dangerous.
scheme: B1: (a) acid rain from sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides corrodes the marble (calcium carbonate)
B1: (b) fertilisers cause an algal bloom; when the algae die, their decay by bacteria uses up the dissolved oxygen (eutrophication)
B1: (c) radiation damages DNA, causing mutations, cancer and birth defects

long.q: State two harmful effects of noise pollution and one way of reducing it.
scheme: B1: it can cause loss of hearing
B1: it causes stress, headaches, sleeplessness and high blood pressure
B1: fitting silencers to vehicles and machines, limiting loudspeakers, or planting trees as sound barriers
